title: Hawk Fire: Human-caused wildfire near Reno, Nevada, prompts state of emergency as 90,000 urged to flee | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Flamescould be seenrapidly advancing down a hillside toward residential neighborhoods near Reno, Nevada, on Sunday, marking the latest in adestructive fire seasonthat has scorched thousands of acres and forced the evacuations of entire towns across the Southwest.

Officials say the uncontained Hawk Fire northwest of Reno was human-caused, but did not say how it started or whether it was intentionally set.

Since igniting Saturday, the fast-moving blaze has scorched more than 15,000 acres and was 0% contained as of Sunday evening, according to fire officials.

Around 90,000 residents are urged to evacuate and at least two medical centers have evacuated patients.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo has declared a state of emergency in Washoe County, which includes Reno and parts of Lake Tahoe, and activated the Nevada National Guard.

“This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant,” Lombardowrote on X. He urged those who were asked to evacuate to do so immediately.

Six people have been injured, including three civilians and three first responders, said Shane Akerson of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District. None of the injuries are life-threatening, Reno Fire Chief David Cochran told CNN’s Erica Hill on Sunday.

There is no indication the fire was intentionally set, but the specific cause remains under investigation, Cochran told CNN.

As of Sunday afternoon, 42,000 people were under mandatory evacuation orders, said Akerson, one of three unified incident commanders, in a news conference. An additional 45,000 people were in yellow evacuation warning zones that should be prepared to leave, according to Akerson.

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam urged residents in the yellow zones to evacuate early if possible to avoid potential traffic jams leaving the heavily populated area.

The evacuation zone had reached the edge of the University of Nevada campus as of Sunday evening. University officials said the campus remains safe and has an emergency response and evacuation plan in place if conditions change, according to astatement.

Northwest Specialty Hospital, in the evacuation warning area, had started evacuating patients due to the nearby wildfire, according to a news release. The hospital is working with emergency responders to close the facility and notifying families of affected patients.

“The safety and well-being of our rehabilitation and behavioral health patients and staff remain the highest priority and we are evacuating out of an abundance of caution,” the hospital said in a statement.

The emergency room at North Valleys, an extension of Northern Nevada Medical Center, also temporarily closed because of a mandated evacuation due to the Hawk Fire, it said in astatement.

Washoe County School Districtannouncedall classes, events and activities would be canceled on Monday at nearly all schools in the district.

The wildfire grew rapidly Saturday, driven by gusty winds, low humidity and dry brush. About 1,000 personnel have been battling the blaze, officials said, but the high winds have complicated efforts to contain it.

Temperatures and winds typically drop overnight in Nevada, giving wildfires a chance to settle and firefighters an opportunity to contain the blaze, according to Cochran. But the Hawk Fire has been difficult to contain because neither temperatures nor winds eased Saturday night like they usually do, Cochran explained.

“It just makes it hard to get your arms around a fire of this size and this magnitude,” he said.

There are assessments underway to determine how many structures have been lost to the fire, Akerson added. Around 10,000 people were without power in Washoe County as of Sunday evening, according to poweroutage.us.

Cari Kieffer toldThe Associated Pressshe saw a video posted on social media that showed her house burned down, with only a scorched basketball hoop still standing.

“I woke up this morning and just started crying — all my kids, they lost everything,” Kieffer said Sunday. “We lost all our stuff. Everything we own is gone.”

Kieffer said her family rushed home from her son’s football game Saturday to save their dogs and whatever possessions they could grab after learning their home was in an evacuation zone.

“I kept looking outside and the flames just kept getting closer and closer every time I looked,” Kieffer told the outlet. “I was like, ‘we gotta go like now.’”

Tyler Duvall, who went camping over the weekend, told the AP the fire was so small Saturday morning that he wasn’t concerned, but by the next day, his house was in the evacuation zone.

“The wind really blew it up,” Duvall said.

After returning from a weekend hunting trip, David Barb found he lost his taxidermy shop, but his house nearby appeared to have been spared thanks to workers with a landscaping company who cut a fire break, he said. His wife was home when the fire started on the other side of the mountain and later evacuated to a friend’s house.

“I’m kind of devastated, but thank God everyone’s safe,” he said Sunday, according to the AP.

Ken McNeil commended the efforts of firefighters, who are using airtankers to douse the flames. “I think they’re doing a great job. That’s an inaccessible area,” McNeil told CNN affiliate KTVN. “They’re using a lot of aircraft, and that’s what you have to do to fight this fire.”

Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve told CNN she’s grateful for all of the support the city has received from both federal and state partners.

“It’s just been all hands on deck. Everyone has been working together with ‘what do you need? What do you need?’” Schieve said Sunday.

“The wonderful thing is we all come together in a big way,” she added.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Sunday his team was keeping track of the situation near the Nevada-California border.

“We’re closely monitoring the #HawkFire across the Tahoe region and Nevada, with state and local partners deployed and coordinating on the ground and in the air,” he saidon X. “Residents in impacted areas should continue following guidance from local emergency officials.”

Poor humidity recovery Sunday night could make it difficult for firefighters to make progress overnight into Monday morning. Smoke is expected to settle into the Reno-Sparks area overnight, reducing visibility and worsening air quality, before dispersing around midday Monday.

Southwest winds will strengthen Monday afternoon, with gusts reaching 20 to 25 mph while conditions remain dry. The combination could make the fire more active and complicate containment efforts.

Even stronger winds are possible Tuesday through Thursday, when gusts could reach 35 mph, or 40 mph in wind-prone areas.

This story has been updated with additional information

CNN’s Avni Trivedi and Tyler Ory contributed to this report.
